result:
Lichens grow on the gravestones of most old cemeteries, and almost nobody looks at them. I think they deserve a look.

A lichen is not one organism. It is a fungus that houses algae or cyanobacteria inside its body, living on the sugars they make from sunlight and giving them shelter and water in return. The partnership is so tight that naturalists long classified lichens as single plants. When the Swiss botanist Simon Schwendener proposed their dual nature in 1867, many colleagues were offended. One mocked the idea as an unnatural union between a captive algal damsel and a tyrant fungal master.

What I like most about them is their pace. Some crustose species on Arctic rock expand by less than a millimeter a year, so a patch the size of a dinner plate can be many centuries old, and a few are thought to have lived for thousands of years. Geologists put this to use. If you know the growth rate, you can measure the largest lichen on a boulder and estimate when a glacier dropped it there. The technique is called lichenometry, and it works because the lichen is so reliably slow.

They are also tough in strange ways. Lichens spent eighteen months outside the International Space Station, exposed to vacuum and raw ultraviolet light, and resumed photosynthesis after coming home. Yet many die quickly in polluted air, so a tree trunk covered in them is good news about what you are breathing.

Next time you pass a stone wall, check it. The gray-green crust may be the oldest living thing on the street.
